request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Switchboard operator, male, 1st year

Interviewer: You came here from another part of the country. How are you getting on with your colleagues?

Interviewee: Really well, haha. Everyone loves a joke. I’m from Guangdong and I’ve got a bit of an accent when I speak Mandarin, so my team leader gave me the nickname Little Canton, and now the whole front office calls me that. Sometimes when I’m on the phone, someone next to me imitates the way I talk, copying how I say ‘shi’ as ‘hai’. Everyone laughs, and I laugh along too, haha, it’s just a bit of fun. At the last department dinner everyone was chatting in the local dialect and having a great time. I couldn’t really understand, so I just ate on the side. My team leader said, Little Canton, can you understand? If you can’t, just eat more. Everyone laughed again for a bit, and I laughed too. I ate quite a lot that night, and my stomach was a bit upset when I got back. They seem to go hiking together at weekends, and there’s a group chat too. Sometimes everyone looks at their phones and laughs together. I don’t seem to be in it. They probably just forgot to add me. Little things like that don’t matter. My team leader says all new people get joked about a bit, they went through the same thing themselves, and taking it seriously would spoil the fun. I think so too. If you take it seriously, you just look petty. Now every day after work, I practise my Mandarin in the dorm with a read-along app on my phone, for an hour. I’ve been doing it for almost three months, and I’ve improved quite a lot. Now when someone imitates the way I talk, I correct myself straight away and say it again. There’s a front-desk vacancy next month. I was going to apply, but then I thought about it and decided to get my Mandarin sorted out first.
